text: Today, as many as nine out of ten people breathe polluted air, leading to some 7 million premature deaths each year. Unless we act decisively, this number could double by 2050.
This is an interactive document. The contents buttons allow you to navigate through the different sections of the report.

We provide open, free-of-charge, consistent and qualitycontrolled information and data products related to air quality and health, solar energy, greenhouse gases and climate forcing, everywhere in the world.
01.1 ─ WHAT IS THE COPERNICUS ATMOSPHERE MONITORING SERVICE (CAMS) 01.2 ─ TAP INTO A WORLD OF ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION
01.1 ─ WHAT IS THE COPERNICUS ATMOSPHERE MONITORING SERVICE (CAMS)
The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) provides consistent information on atmospheric composition anywhere in the world.
Implemented by ECMWF, CAMS is the atmosphere monitoring service of Copernicus, the European Union’s Earth observation programme.

Many of today’s environmental concerns, such as the increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases, the hole in the ozone layer, the health implications of breathing polluted air, the supply of energy by solar plants and safe air transportation depend on the composition of the atmosphere.

The service exploits observations from satellites, as well as sensors on the ground, in the oceans and in the air together with computer models to produce analyses of current conditions and forecasts for the days ahead.
Delivering daily information on the air we breathe.
Providing historical data on solar radiation to support the renewable energy sector.
Compiling emission data of wildfires and net fluxes of greenhouse gases (CO , CH and N O) at the Earth’s surface, to understand climate change.
Providing tools and assessment reports to help policymakers in Europe.
Ensuring quality assurance for its products.
Offering an Atmosphere Data Store (ADS), which provides a single point of access to a variety of atmosphere environmental datasets.
United Nations Framework on Climate Change Convention
CAMS is truly an international and collaborative effort involving over 200 entities distributed in over 30 European countries and elsewhere.
01.2 ─ TAP INTO A WORLD OF ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION
The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) provides free and open access to quality-assured, traceable data and applications.
2. Forecasts for the next few days
Sand and dust stirred up by desert storms over north Africa in March 2018 © contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data processed by ESA Sentinel-3
CAMS monitors and forecasts European air quality, as well as the long-range transport of pollutants worldwide.
The quality of air can significantly impact our health and the environment.
1 – Breathing poor quality air is harmful
2 – Forecasting the transport of pollution around the world
With each breath, we inhale small amounts of potentially harmful gases and microscopic particles. These can directly affect our health.

The transport of pollution across long distances makes air quality a global problem. We combine in-situ and satellite observations with our computer models of the atmosphere to provide daily forecasts of the composition of the atmosphere worldwide.
3 – Providing daily air quality information to millions of people
Our forecasts can be used as input to a wide range of downstream services, such as national air quality forecasts, smartphone applications and policy tools to reach millions of users.

image_footnote: CAMS European air quality (PM10) ensemble forecast for 30 May 2022

text: CAMS provides information about emissions for use in air quality and climate models.
The composition of the atmosphere is driven by the exchange of pollutants and natural substances between Earth’s surface and the air above.
1 – What is the atmosphere made of?

Besides main constituents (nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), argon (0.9%) and carbon dioxide (0.04%)), air also contains trace amounts of other constituents emitted or absorbed through natura and anthropogenic processes. Accounting for these exchanges is crucial to accurately describe the composition of the atmosphere in weather and climate models.

Our catalogues of emission data are based on a combination of existing datasets and new information. They describe emissions from several human and natural sources, including fossil fuel use, ships, aircraft, volcanoes, vegetation and soil, using statistical information provided by individual countries.

We provide information on carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide and methane Earth’s surface fluxes using satellite and in situ observations. Additionally, every day we estimate the emission of aerosols, chemical species and greenhouse gases from biomass burning and wildfires using satellite observations.

image_footnote: CAMS estimates of nitrogen oxide emissions for May 2019

text: CAMS provides information to support the planning of installations, from solar farms to rooftop panels.
Solar energy is making a rapidly growing contribution to the global energy market.
1 – Solar power is becoming more popular
2 – How much solar energy is available?
Solar energy is becoming an increasingly important source of renewable energy in Europe and around the world, with the number of new farm and rooftop solar installations growing rapidly every year.

The amount of available solar radiation at a specific location primarily depends on the season, time of day and the location’s latitude. However, the availability of sunshine is also affected by clouds, aerosol particles, ozone molecules and water vapour in the atmosphere.
3 – Information to support solar energy generation

We combine data from satellites with models of the atmosphere to provide information about how much solar radiation gets through the atmosphere to reach Earth’s surface in support of the solar energy sector, as well as policymakers.

image_footnote: Field of solar panels in Bridgwater, United Kingdom, October 2017

text: CAMS monitors stratospheric ozone and provides forecasts of associated ground-level ultraviolet radiation.
The ozone layer protects us from potentially harmful ultraviolet radiation by absorbing it before it reaches Earth’s surface.

Most atmospheric ozone is in a layer in the stratosphere, where it blocks ultraviolet radiation. But over the last few decades, emissions of human-made ozone-depleting substances (ODSs) have resulted in the thinning of the ozone layer, most prominently over Antarctica. While the emissions of most of these ODSs have been phased out under the Montreal Protocol, they still have an impact on the ozone layer due to their longevity in the atmosphere.

We monitor the amount of ozone in the atmosphere and measure the extent and magnitude of the Antarctic ozone hole as it develops and recovers each year, to continuously assess the impact of remaining or new ODSs on the ozone layer. We also provide a historical record of the ozone layer from 2003 to the present combining observations with our computer models.
In addition to this, we monitor and forecast the amount of ultraviolet radiation reaching Earth’s sur face, taking into account the effect of clouds and aerosol particles.
CAMS provides estimates of the effect of aerosols, ozone and greenhouse gases on global warming.
Climate forcing measures how changes in levels of atmospheric gases or particles affect Earth’s energy budget, and global temperature change.

Climate forcing causes an imbalance in Earth’s energy budget due to changing rates of absorption and reflection of solar energy. Climate forcing components include greenhouse gases, aerosols and clouds, as well as land use changes.

Since the industrial era, rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere have increased levels of energy being absorbed whilst human-induced changes in aerosol concentrations have caused more sunlight to be reflected. Overall, energy absorption has been higher than reflection, leading to Earth warming up.
We estimate how much aerosols, ozone, carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases each contribute to global warming. Those estimates form important inputs to IPCC assessment reports.

chart_footnote: Radiative Forcing Components — IPCC, 2021: 6th Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

text: CAMS provides a range of policy tools and assessment reports to help policymakers in Europe reduce air pollution.
Managing issues related to atmospheric composition requires timely and accurate information.
1 – Air pollution is not a local problem
Pollutants can be transported around the world by the wind, so pollution from both within and outside an area can contribute to localised poor air quality.
2 – Monitoring and improving air quality in Europe

Monitoring and improving air quality in Europe is largely driven by European Union legislation with binding limits for key pollutants that impact public health. To manage compliance, countries measure their pollutant levels and emissions.

By looking at air pollution on a European and global scale, we support policymakers at local, national and international levels with reports and interactive tools that describe the evolution of air quality in Europe.

text: 03 A wealth of applications 03.1 ─ HELPING PEOPLE AND BUSINESSES

Over 3000 entities routinely use CAMS data, covering the areas of air quality, policy support, solar energy, the ozone layer and UV radiation, as well as emissions, surface fluxes and estimates of climate forcing.

CAMS provides 18 use cases across its portfolio that demonstrate how our data helps people and businesses adapt to atmospheric conditions. Those applications have a strong multiplier effect on the actual number of users, reaching literally millions.
03 A wealth of applications 03.2 ─ SOME EXAMPLES
CAMS users develop their own downstream applications to address specific needs with free data and information.
Many more applications are available within the community.

BreezoMeter provides intuitive, personalised information on air quality and pollen levels combining big data and machine learning technology. It reaches millions of users via its mobile application, Application Programming Interfaces, and dedicated website.

image_footnote: Mon Toit Solaire is a web-based integrated decision support system for the development of rooftop photovoltaic power generation. Mon Toit Solaire simulates and calculates the energy potential of a photovoltaic (PV) rooftop project and provides users with reliable technical and financial information.

Windy is a leading global weather forecast visualization service, with a huge and constantly growing user base. The service is available on smartphones, tablets and on the web at http://www.windy.com and features 7 CAMS parameters. Well over a million of individual users worldwide have used CAMS layers on Windy, matching 3-5% of all traffic on Windy.com.

text: Reduction in air pollution during the COVID-19 outbreak: this effort aims at quantifying the short-term mortality impacts during the COVID-19 outbreak in a set of European cities, exploring CAMS air pollution regional analyses and forecasts from two different emission scenarios (‘business as usual and ‘lockdown scenario’).
CAMS air quality data and information are used by broadcasters for their forecasts, reaching public audiences worldwide.

CAMS has media partnerships with broadcasters CNN and Euronews, reaching millions of people from across the world. Broadcast several times a day, the Euronews Air Quality forecast offers viewers air quality information for locations across Europe, reaching over 11 million Europeans.

CNN uses CAMS Air Quality data to show the air quality levels and forecasts across many regions of the world, reaching a global audience. With CNN over 23 million Europeans benefit from CAMS data and over 225 million worldwide.

In addition, CAMS reaches millions more through its media outreach activity. Such activity includes environmental event and air quality monitoring newsflashes, data training, dedicated briefings and events, leading to coverage in mainstream newspapers, TV, radio and online news sites worldwide.
04.2 ─ GLOBAL AND REGIONAL ANALYSES AND FORECASTS
Sentinel-5P tropospheric nitrogen dioxide measurements from April 2018 ©contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data, processed by KNMI

CAMS requires access to timely and quality-controlled data streams from a large variety of satellites, as well as in-situ observing networks including those coordinated by the European Environment Agency (EEA).

CAMS is implemented by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA), the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT), EU Agencies, Member States and other Copernicus Services.

image_footnote: European Air Quality Index from the European Environment Agency (EEA)

text: Data used by the automated global and regional production streams for assimilation or verification require processing of raw measurements and transmission in near real-time to ECMWF and other providers of CAMS products.

CAMS uses over 400 million observations every 12 hours from over 90 satellite products including observations of atmospheric composition from geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites such as those from the European Copernicus Sentinel family.
04.2 ─ GLOBAL AND REGIONAL ANALYSES AND FORECASTS
CAMS analyses and forecasts provide users with accurate information across Europe and the entire globe.

The CAMS global analyses and forecasts are generated by ECMWF’s state-of-the-art weather Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) which includes representation of atmospheric composition covering greenhouse gases, reactive gases and aerosols.
1.5 terabytes of data are produced every day.

image_footnote: CAMS NO global forecast on Windy.com

text: The CAMS regional analyses and forecasts provide users with accurate information concerning air quality all over Europe. A multi-model ensemble approach of 9 regional models is applied, allowing to derive products that are more robust and are of better overall quality than those of the individual systems.
Tens of thousands of new maps are produced online daily.
05.1 ─ THE ATMOSPHERE DATA STORE 05.2 ─ OUR USERS
The CAMS Atmosphere Data Store (ADS) is free to use and is a one-stop-shop to access its atmosphere data, API and support.

Our service is providing open access to data and tools related to atmospheric monitoring. We also support our users by providing quality assurance information, and advice on how to use and interpret data.

The Atmosphere Data Store contains a wealth of information about the Earth’s past, present and future atmosphere regarding reactive gases, aerosols, European air quality, the ozone layer, greenhouse gases, emissions and solar radiation, complemented by a catalogue of preview maps and charts.
All CAMS products undergo a systematic Evaluation and Quality Assurance ensuring continuous assessment, traceability and validation of the service elements.
Full documentation is provided on data products and underlying production/ processing systems.
CAMS registered user numbers surpassed 23,000 by March 2022, helping CAMS reach millions more through their use of our free and open data.

The Atmosphere Data Store provides easy, online access to existing datasets through a unified web interface. It is based on open-source technologies and is continually being further developed with help from the users.

Core to our service is the provision of free, full and open access quality-assured data and tools related to atmospheric monitoring. Anyone can view and download our data, and we provide a range of ready-to-use added-value products as well.
On top of registered users, downstream applications and top-tier broadcast media act as multipliers and allow the service to reach hundreds of millions.

text: Easy access to high-quality environmental data has never been more important
1.5 TB of data are downloaded every day from the Atmosphere Data Store.
06.1 ─ A USER DRIVEN PROGRAMME 06.2 ─ USER SUPPORT
CAMS collects and analyses user requirements to trigger new research and development towards the evolution of the Service.

As key policy customers, the European Commission and EU Member States rely on CAMS in several European policy areas. CAMS ensures consistent messaging and data access for European policy makers and agencies in need of environmental information.

Of paramount importance is also the consistency with and contribution to broader international initiatives conducted under the aegis of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

As a User-driven programme, CAMS engages with policy makers, industry, academia and other stakeholders in Europe and elsewhere to identify new requirements to continuously develop and improve the CAMS product portfolio, applications and services to meet and exceed customer expectations.
Requirements are recorded and analysed on a regular basis to trigger new research and development lines and subsequent CAMS Service Evolution.
CHANNELS FOR GATHERING REQUIREMENTS → FEEDBACK VIA USER SUPPORT CHANNELS
CAMS provides a range of channels for getting the necessary help and support.
We are committed to helping users make the most of our open data through the provision of timely, consistently high quality and professional support with every customer contact.
Nearly all CAMS helpdesk tickets are attended to within 8 hours and are generally (>95%) closed within 5 working days.
Thousands of people have been trained on CAMS products and services. User satisfaction reaches 4.7/5.

Besides extensive on-line documentation, CAMS organizes and contributes regularly to training events in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA) and the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorologica Satellites (EUMETSAT).
Volcanic eruption from Fuego volcano, Guatemala, June 2018
In its second phase, CAMS will evolve further with exciting new service components.

The continuous evolution of service and infrastructure is vital to harness science progress, exploit new technologies, and maintain the highest quality of products to meet emerging policy requirements and develop new market opportunities.

CAMS will host an anthropogenic CO Monitoring and Verification Support (MVS) capacity, providing the European Union with a comprehensive picture of actual emissions levels and their reduction worldwide. The system will rely on data from the upcoming EU CO2M satellite mission enabling the detection of emitting hot spots such as megacities or power plants.
It will integrate emissions from observations (space and in-situ), prior information (from emission inventories and reporting) and modelling and data assimilation capabilities.
CAMS for the next 7 years (2021 - 2028) will ensure the enhanced continuity of the service, including some significant novel elements.
CAMS represents an invaluable resource for the implementation of the Green Deal, a priority of the European Commission, and the EU commitment to achieving zero pollution.

The CAMS product offering will be expanded. Global and regional atmosphere products will be continuously improved by ensuring the timely uptake of new observations such as those from the European Sentinel-4 and Sentinel-5 satellites. Enhanced atmospheric composition modelling will allow increased spatial resolution and time span, and exploitation of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques.
A dedicated National Collaboration Programme will enable each country to benefit from CAMS support to fulfil their environmental and climate obligations.

Copernicus efforts at ECMWF will further benefit from powerful synergies with C3S and Destination Earth (DestinE), a new programme of the Commission to develop very high precision digital twins of the Earth to monitor and simulate natural and human activity.

The CAMS mission represents an invaluable resource for the implementation of the European Green Deal, which has been established as a priority of the European Commission, committed to a cross-cutting zero-pollution strategy.
